questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the literal meaning of cài?
Which pattern is used when one thing is LESS than another?
What does the pattern mean without the negative méi-?
What must suīrán always be followed by?
Where may suīrán be placed in a sentence?
Write the Chinese for "He isn't as busy as you."
Write the Chinese for "Although she likes to travel, she has never been to China."

answers.answer_text: Suīrán tā xǐhuan lǚxíng, kěshi tā méi qùguo Zhōngguó.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Is kěshi usually translated into English?

answers.answer_text: No — though sometimes the word "still" is included in the translation.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I'm not as clever as he is."
What kinds of dish does cài include?

answers.answer_text: Both meat and vegetable dishes — any dish eaten with rice.

articles.text:
2. B: Dōngménde cài kǒngpà méiyou    I'm afraid that the food at the East
      Dàhuáde cài nàme hǎo ba.        Gate isn't as good as the food at
                                       the Great China.
   A: Suīrán bú tài hǎo, kěshi lí    Even though it (East Gate) is not
      wǒmen zhèli jìn.                too good, it is close to us.

Notes on No. 2

Cài, "(nonstaple) food," "dish," "course (of a meal)": Literally, cài means "vegetables." It refers to any dish that is eaten with rice. Both meat and vegetable dishes are included in the meaning.

The pattern ...(méi)yǒu...nàme... is used to make comparisons when one thing is LESS than another.

ITEM 1 + méiyou + ITEM 2 + nàme/zhème + STATE VERB (OFTEN ADJECTIVAL VERB)

Tā méiyou nǐ nàme máng.          He isn't as busy as you.
Wǒ méiyou ta nàme cōngming.      I'm not as clever as he is.
Tā méiyou wǒ nàme yǒu qián.      He isn't as rich as I am.

Used less frequently without the negative méi-, the pattern means "to be as (quality) AS (something else)."

Nǐde shū méiyou wǒde shū         Your books are not as many as mine.
nàme duō.                        (You don't have as many books as I do.)
Yǒu.                             Yes, they are.
Nèige xuéxiàode túshūguǎn yǒu    Is that school's library as good as
zhèige xuéxiàode zhème hǎo ma?   this one's?

Suīrán...kěshi...: Suīrán, "although," must always be followed by kěshi or dànshi, meaning "but," in the second part of a sentence. Kěshi/dànshi would not usually be translated into English, but sometimes the word "still" is included in the translation. Suīrán may either precede the subject or be placed between the subject and the verb of a sentence.

Suīrán tā xǐhuan lǚxíng, kěshi   Although she likes to travel, she
tā méi qùguo Zhōngguó.           has never been to China.
Tā suīrán jiǎngle hǎojǐcì,       Although he explained it many times,
kěshi wǒ háishi bù dǒng.         I still didn't understand.
